From a controller board to a motor command

I worked on both the controller hardware and the software that sends commands to the robot’s motors.

I co-developed the schematic from an open-source architecture and worked with teammates on PCB layout. After fabrication, I hand-assembled, reworked, and bench-tested the prototype. I also built Python and C++ tools for communicating with the robot’s motor drivers.

Schematic, PCB, and assembly

Berkeley Humanoid Lite and Recoil provided the starting architecture and firmware. My work focused on adapting the schematic and packaging, contributing to the PCB layout, and developing the host-side interface.

Communication and control

My host-side tools send commands over SocketCAN and collect telemetry and fault logs. I used watchdogs, command limits, readbacks, and isolated tests to trace problems in wiring, adapters, firmware timing, and behavior under load.

Position, velocity, and feedforward torque
τ = Kp(qdes − q) + Kd(q̇des − q̇) + τff

The custom Recoil mode combines position and velocity feedback with a feedforward torque command. Its interface uses output-joint radians, radians per second, and newton-metres, carried in a custom packet format.

Board bring-up and the next revision

PROJECT STATUS

The first custom board did not work.

After fabrication, assembly, rework, and bench testing, I was unable to get the first custom FOC board operating. I continued the robot integration with off-the-shelf drivers and used the board-debugging work to plan the next revision, with closer checks of power, sensing, wiring, and firmware bring-up.

The custom board, the Recoil firmware work, and the motor-driver interface are separate parts of the project. The robot’s progress with off-the-shelf drivers is described on the quadruped page.
